ch40.title: Lazarus, Come Forth
ch40.b002: From February 11 to 20, Jesus and the twelve toured the cities and villages of northern Perea where Abner’s associates and the women’s corps were at work. Everywhere the messengers were meeting with success, and Jesus kept pointing out to his apostles that the gospel could spread without the accompaniment of miracles and wonders. On the Sabbath, February 18, at Ragaba, a wealthy Pharisee named Nathaniel gave a breakfast for some twenty of his fellow Pharisees who were following Jesus about the country, and invited the Master as guest of honor. Jesus went straight to his seat at the left of the host without going to the water basins to wash his hands. Many of the Pharisees knew that he washed only for cleanliness and abhorred purely ceremonial performances, but Nathaniel was shocked.
ch40.b003: After much whispering between the host and an unfriendly Pharisee on his right, and much lifting of eyebrows and sneering curling of lips across the table, Jesus spoke. He had thought, he said, that they had invited him to break bread and inquire about the gospel, but they had brought him to witness “⟦Q 166:1.3⟧an exhibition of ceremonial devotion to your own self-righteousness.⟦/Q⟧” Then: “⟦Q 166:1.4⟧How carefully you cleanse the outside of the cups and the platters while the spiritual-food vessels are filthy and polluted!… Woe upon all who shun justice, spurn mercy, and reject truth!⟦/Q⟧” When a lawyer asked whether there was nothing good in the scribes and lawyers, Jesus, standing, rebuked those who laid heavy burdens on men’s shoulders and would not lift them with one finger, and who had “⟦Q 166:1.5⟧taken away the key of knowledge from the common people.⟦/Q⟧” Then he went out of the house without partaking of food. Some of those Pharisees became believers; the larger number grew all the more determined to catch some word of his that could bring him before the Sanhedrin.
ch40.b005: The next day, as Jesus and the twelve approached Amathus near the border of Samaria, they met ten lepers, nine Jews and one Samaritan. Ordinarily the Jews would have shunned the Samaritan, but their common affliction had overcome all prejudice. The seventy had announced that Jesus would pass this way, and the lepers had posted themselves outside the city. Not daring to come near, they stood afar off and cried: “⟦Q 166:2.1⟧Master, have mercy on us; cleanse us from our affliction. Heal us as you have healed others.⟦/Q⟧”
ch40.b006: When Simon Zelotes saw the Samaritan among them, he urged the Master to go on into the city without even greeting them. Jesus said: “⟦Q 166:2.3⟧But what if the Samaritan loves God as well as the Jews? Should we sit in judgment on our fellow men? Who can tell? if we make these ten men whole, perhaps the Samaritan will prove more grateful even than the Jews. Do you feel certain about your opinions, Simon?⟦/Q⟧” Simon replied, “⟦Q 166:2.3⟧If you cleanse them, you will soon find out.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus went near the lepers and told them to go and show themselves to the priests as the law of Moses required, and as they went, they were made whole. The nine Jews, grateful as they were, continued on their way to the priests. But the Samaritan turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice, and fell on his knees at Jesus’ feet to give thanks.
ch40.b007: The Master looked about at the twelve, especially at Simon Zelotes, and said: “⟦Q 166:2.5⟧Were not ten cleansed? Where, then, are the other nine, the Jews? Only one, this alien, has returned to give glory to God.⟦/Q⟧” And to the Samaritan: “⟦Q 166:2.5⟧Arise and go your way; your faith has made you whole.⟦/Q⟧” As the stranger departed, Jesus looked again at his apostles. They all looked at Jesus, save Simon Zelotes, whose eyes were downcast. The twelve said not a word. Neither did Jesus speak; it was not necessary that he should. Though all ten believed they had leprosy, only four did; the other six were cured of a skin disease mistaken for it. The Samaritan had really been a leper.
ch40.b008: The Narrow Door and the Tower of Siloam
ch40.b009: At Gerasa a believing Pharisee asked whether few or many would be saved. Jesus answered that salvation is first a matter of personal choosing. “⟦Q 166:3.3⟧Even if the door to the way of life is narrow, it is wide enough to admit all who sincerely seek to enter, for I am that door.⟦/Q⟧” The danger lay in postponing entrance while pursuing the pleasures of immaturity, for to those who refused while the door was open, it would at last be shut. “⟦Q 166:3.5⟧But fear not; every one who sincerely desires to find eternal life by entrance into the kingdom of God shall certainly find such everlasting salvation.⟦/Q⟧”
ch40.b010: At a noontide halt on the way to Philadelphia, Thomas asked whether the angels could prevent accidents. Jesus answered that it was superstition to think prosperity the token of God’s approval and adversity the proof of his displeasure. “⟦Q 166:4.4⟧The Father causes his rain to fall on the just and the unjust.⟦/Q⟧” The Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with the sacrifices, and the eighteen on whom the tower of Siloam fell, were not sinners above their fellows; “⟦Q 166:4.4⟧these folks were simply innocent victims of one of the accidents of time.⟦/Q⟧” And he said: “⟦Q 166:4.10⟧Health is not the smile of heaven, neither is affliction the frown of God.⟦/Q⟧”
ch40.b011: On Wednesday, February 22, Jesus and ten apostles reached Philadelphia with more than six hundred followers. Its synagogue had never been under the Sanhedrin, and Abner was teaching there three times a day. At a Sabbath breakfast in the house of a wealthy Pharisee, a believer swollen with dropsy came in and sat down upon the floor. Jesus asked the learned guests whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath; they held their peace. He took the man by the hand: “⟦Q 167:1.5⟧Arise and go your way. You have not asked to be healed, but I know the desire of your heart and the faith of your soul.⟦/Q⟧” Then he counseled them, when bidden to a feast, to take the lowest place, “⟦Q 167:5.1⟧for every one who exalts himself shall be humbled,⟦/Q⟧” and to invite sometimes the poor, the maimed, and the blind, who could not repay them. That day, in the synagogue, he saw an elderly woman bent over, who for more than eighteen years had been bowed down by fear. Touching her shoulder, he said: “⟦Q 167:3.1⟧Woman, if you would only believe, you could be wholly loosed from your spirit of infirmity.⟦/Q⟧” She believed and straightened up immediately, glorifying God. When the unfriendly ruler of the synagogue protested against healing on the Sabbath, Jesus asked whether any of them would not loose his ox on the Sabbath and lead it to water; should not this daughter of Abraham be loosed from her bondage? The ruler was put to shame and later deposed.
ch40.b013: Very late on Sunday night, February 26, a runner arrived from Bethany with a message from Martha and Mary: “⟦Q 167:4.1⟧Lord, he whom you love is very sick.⟦/Q⟧” At first Jesus made no reply. There came one of those strange interludes when he seemed to be in communication with something beyond himself. Then he looked up and said to the messenger, in the hearing of the apostles: “⟦Q 167:4.1⟧This sickness is really not to the death. Doubt not that it may be used to glorify God and exalt the Son.⟦/Q⟧”
ch40.b014: Jesus loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus with a fervent affection, and his first human thought was to go to them at once. But another idea came into his mind. He had almost given up hope that the leaders at Jerusalem would accept the kingdom, yet he still loved his people, and he resolved, his Father willing, to give them one more chance, and to make this last appeal to Jerusalem the most stupendous outward working of his entire earth career. The Jews believed that the soul might linger near the body for two or three days, but never after the third, and that no one ever returned from the tomb after that. So Jesus tarried two full days longer in Philadelphia.
ch40.b015: Early on Wednesday morning he said: “⟦Q 167:4.4⟧Let us prepare at once to go into Judea again.⟦/Q⟧” The apostles took counsel and came back as one man, James speaking for them: “⟦Q 167:4.4⟧Master, you were in Jerusalem a few weeks back, and the leaders sought your death, while the people were minded to stone you.… and we will not permit you to go again into Judea.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered: “⟦Q 167:4.5⟧But do you not understand that there are twelve hours of the day in which work may safely be done? If a man walks in the day, he does not stumble inasmuch as he has light.… Besides, do you not realize that our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, and I would go to awake him out of this sleep!⟦/Q⟧” When one of them said that if Lazarus slept he would surely recover, Jesus told them plainly: “Lazarus is dead.” Then Thomas spoke to his fellows: “⟦Q 167:4.7⟧We have told the Master our fears, but he is determined to go to Bethany. I am satisfied it means the end; they will surely kill him, but if that is the Master’s choice, then let us acquit ourselves like men of courage; let us go also that we may die with him.⟦/Q⟧” It was ever so: in matters requiring deliberate and sustained courage, Thomas was the mainstay of the twelve.
ch40.b017: Almost fifty friends and enemies followed Jesus toward Judea. At the noon halt he told them that salvation is a free gift to all who have the faith to receive it, and spoke the parable of the Pharisee and the publican who went up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other men, but the publican, standing afar off, “⟦Q 167:5.1⟧would not so much as lift his eyes to heaven but smote his breast, saying, ‘God be merciful to me a sinner.’ I tell you that the publican went home with God’s approval rather than the Pharisee.⟦/Q⟧” That night at Jericho the Pharisees tried to entrap him on the question of divorce. He skillfully avoided their snare, but he exalted marriage as the highest of human relationships and denounced the lax practices that wronged women and children.
ch40.b018: Word of his teaching spread through Jericho, and the next morning, even before breakfast, scores of mothers came carrying their children in their arms and leading them by the hand, asking that he bless them. When the apostles loudly rebuked them, Jesus came out and indignantly reproved his apostles: “⟦Q 167:6.1⟧Suffer little children to come to me; forbid them not, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.⟦/Q⟧” He received all the children, laying his hands on them, and spoke words of courage and hope to their mothers. Those women little realized that the onlooking intelligences of Nebadon beheld the children of Jericho playing with the Creator of a universe. As they climbed the hills toward Bethany, Nathaniel walked beside Jesus asking about the ministry of angels, until they were interrupted by Martha hurrying out to meet them.
ch40.b019: I Am the Resurrection and the Life
ch40.b020: It was shortly after noon on Thursday. Lazarus had been dead four days; he had been laid in the family tomb at the far end of the garden late on Sunday afternoon, and that very morning the stone had been rolled across the entrance. He had died only a few hours after the messenger left for Philadelphia. Mary had given up hope and was abandoned to her grief, but Martha clung to it, and had set a neighbor lad to watch the Jericho road from the brow of the hill; it was he who brought word that Jesus was coming. Many of the mourners in the house were Jesus’ bitter enemies from Jerusalem, so Martha went out alone.
ch40.b021: She fell at his feet, exclaiming, “⟦Q 168:0.6⟧Master, if you had been here, my brother would not have died!⟦/Q⟧” Jesus lifted her up: “⟦Q 168:0.6⟧Only have faith, Martha, and your brother shall rise again.⟦/Q⟧” Martha answered that she knew he would rise in the resurrection of the last day. Then Jesus, looking straight into her eyes, said: “⟦Q 168:0.7⟧I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, though he dies, yet shall he live. In truth, whosoever lives and believes in me shall never really die. Martha, do you believe this?⟦/Q⟧” And Martha answered: “⟦Q 168:0.7⟧Yes, I have long believed that you are the Deliverer, the Son of the living God, even he who should come to this world.⟦/Q⟧”
ch40.b022: Martha went in and whispered to her sister, “⟦Q 168:0.8⟧The Master is here and has asked for you.⟦/Q⟧” Mary rose quickly and went out, and the mourners, supposing she was going to the tomb to weep, followed her. Mary fell at Jesus’ feet with the same cry: “⟦Q 168:0.10⟧If you had only been here, my brother would not have died!⟦/Q⟧” When Jesus saw how they all grieved, his soul was moved with compassion. His human mind was mightily stirred by the conflict between his love for Lazarus and the sisters and his disdain for the outward show of mourning by some who in their hearts were bent on his death.
ch40.b023: The Tomb at the End of the Garden
ch40.b024: “Where have you laid him?” he asked. Martha said, “Come and see.” And as the Master followed in silence with the two sisters, he wept. One of the friendly Jews said: “⟦Q 168:1.1⟧Behold how he loved him. Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind have kept this man from dying?⟦/Q⟧” His enemies sneered: if he thought so much of the man, why had he tarried so long? Why Jesus wept is hard to explain. He felt a deep human sympathy for the sisters; he was troubled by the crowd of mourners, some sincere, some pretenders; and he truly hesitated to summon his friend back to mortal life, knowing the bitter persecution Lazarus would endure for being the subject of the greatest demonstration of his power. They stood before the tomb, a small natural cave in the ledge of rock that rose some thirty feet at the far end of the garden. It was about half past two on Thursday afternoon.
ch40.b025: Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha hesitated: “⟦Q 168:1.12⟧Must we roll away the stone? My brother has now been dead four days, so that by this time decay of the body has begun.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered: “⟦Q 168:1.12⟧Did I not tell you at the first that this sickness was not to the death? Have I not come to fulfill my promise? And after I came to you, did I not say that, if you would only believe, you should see the glory of God? Wherefore do you doubt?⟦/Q⟧” Then the apostles, with willing neighbors, rolled the stone away. The forty-five or so who stood there could dimly see the form of Lazarus, wrapped in linen bandages, on the right lower niche of the cave. They little realized that, near at hand, a vast concourse of celestial beings, assembled under Gabriel, waited to execute the bidding of their Sovereign.
ch40.b026: Jesus lifted up his eyes and said: “⟦Q 168:2.2⟧Father, I am thankful that you heard and granted my request. I know that you always hear me, but because of those who stand here with me, I thus speak with you, that they may believe that you have sent me into the world, and that they may know that you are working with me in that which we are about to do.⟦/Q⟧” And when he had prayed, he cried with a loud voice:
ch40.b028: In just twelve seconds of earth time the lifeless form began to move and sat up on the edge of the stone shelf, bound about with grave cloths, his face covered with a napkin. As he stood up before them, alive, Jesus said, “⟦Q 168:2.3⟧Loose him and let him go.⟦/Q⟧” All but the apostles and the two sisters fled to the house, pale with fright. Lazarus asked the meaning of the grave cloths and why he had awakened in the garden, and Martha told him that he had died on Sunday and was now brought back on Thursday; he had had no consciousness of time. Then he knelt with his sisters at the Master’s feet. Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up: “⟦Q 168:2.7⟧My son, what has happened to you will also be experienced by all who believe this gospel except that they shall be resurrected in a more glorious form. You shall be a living witness of the truth which I spoke—I am the resurrection and the life. But let us all now go into the house and partake of nourishment for these physical bodies.⟦/Q⟧” Gabriel made record of the first instance on Urantia, and the last, where a mortal had been resurrected in the likeness of the physical body of death.
ch40.b030: By noon the next day the story had spread over all Jerusalem. At one o’clock that Friday the Sanhedrin met, and after more than two hours of bitter debate a Pharisee moved that Jesus be put to death at once, without trial. The resolution never came to a vote, for fourteen members resigned in a body and never sat in the council again. Later five more were thrown out for friendliness toward Jesus, and with these nineteen gone the Sanhedrin could condemn him with a solidarity bordering on unanimity. At this meeting Caiaphas the high priest first spoke the old adage he was to repeat so often: “⟦Q 168:3.6⟧It is better that one man die, than that the community perish.⟦/Q⟧”
ch40.b031: Warned of all this, Jesus was not in the least perturbed; he rested over the Sabbath with friends at Bethpage, near Bethany, and early Sunday took leave of the Bethany family and set out for Pella. On the way the apostles kept returning to his words, “⟦Q 168:4.2⟧This sickness is not really to the death,⟦/Q⟧” spoken when Lazarus had already been dead eleven hours. Jesus taught them that no sincere prayer is denied an answer, and that delay often betokens a better answer. Lazarus remained at Bethany until the days of the crucifixion, when, warned that the Sanhedrin had decreed his death too, he fled to Abner at Philadelphia, and his sisters soon followed. He became treasurer of the church there and died at sixty-seven of the same sickness that had carried him off as a younger man at Bethany.
ch41.title: The Son Who Was Lost
ch41.b002: Late on Monday evening, March 6, Jesus and the ten apostles arrived back at the Pella camp. Word of Lazarus’s resurrection had come two days before them, and the whole encampment was agog; nothing since the feeding of the five thousand had so stirred the imagination of the people. This was to be the last week of Jesus’ stay at Pella, and he was very active. Every afternoon he preached to the crowds, and every night he answered the questions of the apostles and the more advanced disciples living in the camp. It was at the very height of this second, nonmiraculous phase of the kingdom’s ministry that he meant to teach this one short week and then set out through southern Perea on the road that led to Jerusalem.
ch41.b003: Meanwhile the Pharisees and the chief priests were shaping their charges. He was, they said, a friend of publicans and sinners, who received the ungodly and even ate with them. He was a blasphemer, who spoke of God as his Father and thought himself equal with God. He was a lawbreaker, who healed on the Sabbath and in many other ways flouted the sacred law of Israel. And he was in league with devils, working his wonders by the power of Beelzebub, the prince of devils.
ch41.b004: The Lost Sheep and the Lost Coin
ch41.b005: On Thursday afternoon Jesus spoke to the multitude about the “Grace of Salvation.” The prophets from Samuel to John, he said, had always urged men to seek God: “⟦Q 169:1.2⟧Seek the Lord while he may be found.⟦/Q⟧” And that teaching should be taken to heart. “⟦Q 169:1.2⟧But I have come to show you that, while you are seeking to find God, God is likewise seeking to find you.⟦/Q⟧” He reminded them of the good shepherd who left the ninety and nine in the fold to go after the one that was lost, and carried it tenderly home on his shoulder, calling his friends to rejoice with him. “The fact that souls are lost only increases the interest of the heavenly Father. I have come to this world to do my Father’s bidding, and it has truly been said of the Son of Man that he is a friend of publicans and sinners.
ch41.b006: “⟦Q 169:1.3⟧You have been taught that divine acceptance comes after your repentance and as a result of all your works of sacrifice and penitence, but I assure you that the Father accepts you even before you have repented and sends the Son and his associates to find you and bring you, with rejoicing, back to the fold, the kingdom of sonship and spiritual progress. You are all like sheep which have gone astray, and I have come to seek and to save those who are lost.⟦/Q⟧”
ch41.b007: Then he told again of the woman who had ten pieces of silver made into a necklace and lost one of them, and who lit the lamp and swept the house diligently until she found it, and then called her friends and neighbors: “⟦Q 169:1.4⟧Rejoice with me, for I have found the piece that was lost.⟦/Q⟧” The Son of Man, he said, goes out into the wilderness after the straying sheep, but he also searches for the coin lost in the house. “⟦Q 169:1.4⟧The sheep wanders away, unintentionally; the coin is covered by the dust of time and obscured by the accumulation of the things of men.⟦/Q⟧” And now, he said, he would tell of a thoughtless son of a well-to-do farmer who left his father’s house deliberately. “⟦Q 169:1.5⟧You recall that the sheep strayed away without intention, but this youth left his home with premeditation.⟦/Q⟧”
ch41.b009: “⟦Q 169:1.6⟧A certain man had two sons.⟦/Q⟧” The younger was lighthearted and carefree, always seeking a good time and shirking responsibility; the elder was serious, hard-working, and willing to bear burdens, but self-centered, surly, and conceited. The two were always quarreling and bickering. The younger enjoyed play but shunned work; the older devoted himself to work but seldom played. At last the younger came to his father and said: “⟦Q 169:1.6⟧Father, give me the third portion of your possessions which would fall to me and allow me to go out into the world to seek my own fortune.⟦/Q⟧” And the father, knowing how unhappy the young man was at home and with his brother, divided his property and gave the youth his share.
ch41.b010: Within a few weeks the young man gathered together all he had and set out for a far country. Finding nothing profitable to do which was also pleasurable, he soon wasted his whole inheritance in riotous living. And when he had spent everything, a prolonged famine arose in that land, and he found himself in want. In his hunger and distress he hired himself to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into the fields to feed swine. He would gladly have filled himself with the husks the swine ate, but no one would give him anything.
ch41.b011: One day, when he was very hungry, he came to himself and said: “⟦Q 169:1.8⟧How many hired servants of my father have bread enough and to spare while I perish with hunger, feeding swine off here in a foreign country! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no more worthy to be called your son; only be willing to make me one of your hired servants.⟦/Q⟧” And having reached this decision, he arose and set out for his father’s house.
ch41.b012: While He Was Yet Afar Off
ch41.b013: Now the father had grieved much for his son. He had missed the cheerful, thoughtless lad; he loved him and was always on the lookout for his return. So on the day the son came near, while he was still far off, the father saw him, and moved with loving compassion, he ran out to meet him and embraced and kissed him. The son looked up into his father’s tearful face and began: “⟦Q 169:1.9⟧Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight; I am no more worthy to be called a son⟦/Q⟧”—but he never finished his confession, for the overjoyed father called to the servants who had come running: “⟦Q 169:1.9⟧Bring quickly his best robe, the one I have saved, and put it on him and put the son’s ring on his hand and fetch sandals for his feet.⟦/Q⟧”
ch41.b014: When the happy father had led the footsore and weary lad into the house, he called again: “⟦Q 169:1.10⟧Bring on the fatted calf and kill it, and let us eat and make merry, for this my son was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.⟦/Q⟧” And the whole household gathered about the father to rejoice with him over the restoration of his son.
ch41.b015: About this time the elder son came in from his day’s work in the field. As he drew near the house he heard music and dancing, and at the back door he called a servant and asked what it meant. The servant told him that his long-lost brother had come home, and that their father had killed the fatted calf to celebrate his safe return. The elder brother was so hurt and angry that he would not go in. His father came out to entreat him, but he would not yield. “⟦Q 169:1.12⟧Here these many years have I served you, never transgressing the least of your commands, and yet you never gave me even a kid that I might make merry with my friends.… but when this your son returns, having squandered your substance with harlots, you make haste to kill the fatted calf and make merry over him.⟦/Q⟧”
ch41.b016: Since this father truly loved both his sons, he reasoned with the elder: “⟦Q 169:1.13⟧But, my son, you have all the while been with me, and all this which I have is yours. You could have had a kid at any time you had made friends to share your merriment. But it is only proper that you should now join with me in being glad and merry because of your brother’s return. Think of it, my son, your brother was lost and is found; he has returned alive to us!⟦/Q⟧”
ch41.b017: Jesus loved to tell these three stories together. The lost sheep showed that when men stray unintentionally from the path of life, the Father goes out with his Sons, the true shepherds, to seek them. The lost coin showed how thorough is the divine search for those confused or spiritually blinded by the cares and accumulations of life. And the lost son showed how complete is the restoration of the returning prodigal to his Father’s house and heart. Many, many times during his years of teaching Jesus told and retold this story, and it and the story of the good Samaritan were his favorite means of teaching the love of the Father and the neighborliness of man.
ch41.b019: One evening Simon Zelotes asked what the Master had meant that day by saying that the children of the world are often wiser in their generation than the children of the kingdom, since they are skillful in making friends with the mammon of unrighteousness. Jesus told of a rich man whose steward had oppressed the clients and squandered the funds, and who was ordered to give an account and hand over his office. The steward said to himself: “⟦Q 169:2.4⟧What shall I do since I am about to lose this stewardship? I have not the strength to dig; to beg I am ashamed.⟦/Q⟧” So he called in his master’s debtors one by one. To the man who owed a hundred measures of oil he said, “⟦Q 169:2.4⟧Take your wax board bond, sit down quickly, and change it to fifty⟦/Q⟧”; to the one who owed a hundred measures of wheat, “⟦Q 169:2.4⟧Take your bond and write fourscore.⟦/Q⟧” Even his master, when he found out, had to admit that the unfaithful steward had shown sagacity in providing for his days of want.
ch41.b020: If they had been so diligent in serving themselves before they entered the kingdom, Jesus asked, why should they be less diligent now in gaining souls, as stewards of God? “⟦Q 169:2.6,169:2.7⟧I affirm that he who is faithful in little will also be faithful in much, while he who is unrighteous in little will also be unrighteous in much.… You cannot serve God and mammon.⟦/Q⟧” The Pharisees present, much given to acquiring riches, began to sneer and scoff and tried to draw him into argument, but he refused to debate with his enemies and went to his tent for the night.
ch41.b021: When the wrangling grew loud, Simon Peter stood up and took charge. This was no new doctrine, he told them, and he reminded them of the old allegory of the Nazarites that John the Baptist used to thunder at those who loved riches. A rich man named Dives, clothed in purple and fine linen, lived in splendor every day, while a beggar named Lazarus lay at his gate, covered with sores, longing for the crumbs from his table. Both died; the beggar was carried to Abraham’s bosom, and the rich man woke in torment and begged that Lazarus be sent to warn his five brothers. But Abraham said: “⟦Q 169:3.2⟧If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded even if one were to rise from the dead.⟦/Q⟧” Then Andrew dismissed the crowd. Though the apostles often asked about this parable, Jesus never consented to comment on it.
ch41.b023: Jesus always had trouble making his apostles understand that, though they proclaimed the kingdom of God, the Father in heaven was not a king. Never did he call his Father a king. In his intimate talks he spoke of himself as the Son of Man and as their elder brother. He never argued for the reality of the Father; he took it for granted. In fact he taught only two things about him: that God in himself is spirit, and that in all his relations with his creatures he is a Father. Men learn about God from Jesus by observing the divinity of his life, not by depending on his teachings; they could never fully understand God, but they could most certainly know him, even as they had known the Son of Man. Never did he say, “⟦Q 169:4.12⟧Whoso has heard me has heard God.⟦/Q⟧” But he did say, “⟦Q 169:4.12⟧He who has seen me has seen the Father.⟦/Q⟧” On one of these evenings he made his final pronouncement of his relationship with God: “⟦Q 169:4.11⟧I have come out from the Father, and I have come into the world; again, I will leave the world and go to the Father.⟦/Q⟧”
ch41.b024: March 11, the Last Sermon at Pella
ch41.b025: On Saturday afternoon, March 11, Jesus preached his last sermon at Pella, a full discussion of the kingdom of heaven. He knew how confused his followers were about the term; the idea of a temporal king and of David’s restored throne was too deep-rooted in them. He made it clear that the kingdom must begin with, and be centered in, the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, and that those who accepted this truth would be freed from the age-long bondage of fear. That afternoon he described two phases of the kingdom: “⟦Q 170:2.18,170:2.19⟧First. The kingdom of God in this world, the supreme desire to do the will of God, the unselfish love of man which yields the good fruits of improved ethical and moral conduct. Second. The kingdom of God in heaven, the goal of mortal believers, the estate wherein the love for God is perfected, and wherein the will of God is done more divinely.⟦/Q⟧”
ch41.b026: By faith, he taught, the believer enters the kingdom now: by coming as a little child, receiving sonship as a gift, and by hungering and thirsting for righteousness. God has already forgiven; men make that forgiveness personally available by forgiving their fellows, and they will not truly forgive unless they love their neighbors as themselves. Right conduct is the natural fruit of such love. He did not put ethics in the place of religion; he taught religion as a cause and ethics as a result. The religion of the kingdom is personal; its fruits are familial and social. On this day he earnestly urged his followers to give up the term kingdom of God in favor of its practical equivalent, the will of God, but he did not succeed. Whatever else he said about the kingdom, his last word to his apostles was always, “The kingdom is within you.”
ch41.b027: In later times his followers set the kingdom off into the future and built in its place a visible church. The church was an inevitable and useful outgrowth of his life and teachings; the tragedy was that it so nearly displaced his spiritual concept of the kingdom, the will of the Father ruling in the heart of each believer. Yet that ideal is not lost. The church, says the record, is only the cocoon in which the kingdom of Jesus’ concept now slumbers, and one day it will come forth.
ch41.b028: By now more than four thousand people gathered each morning to hear Jesus or Peter preach. Three quarters of them were truth seekers; the rest were Pharisees from Jerusalem, doubters, and cavilers. The Master chose to end his work on earth when interest in his message stood at its highest point, the highest reached in this second, nonmiraculous phase of the kingdom. Now he made ready to leave Pella, to go south through Perea, and up at last to Jerusalem.
